Next to the ones you pay for
Where Blazify wins, and where it does not. Both are worth knowing before you install anything.
There are a dozen open-source music players. Here is what is actually different about this one, including the part that is not flattering.

Almost every open-source music player that streams from YouTube is built on the same foundation, and inherits the same worst failure along with it: songs that stop partway through, or refuse to start at all, whenever YouTube changes something at their end. If you have tried one of these apps and quietly given up on it, that is almost certainly what happened.

Most of the work here has gone into that. The player was asking for audio streams it had no way to decode, which guaranteed a refusal on a step that reported no error at all. Two of the three fallback paths had been quietly returning nothing for every song, because the component they depend on was never handed anything to fetch with. Both are fixed. It is an arms race rather than a bug, so what matters is not that it works today but how quickly it gets repaired when it next breaks.

The other difference is reach. Nearly all of them run on one platform. Blazify is one project across Android, Windows, Linux and iPhone, written by one person in Kathmandu, where a dropped connection is ordinary and mobile data is not cheap. That is why the music already on your phone plays beside everything streamed, and why offline was never an afterthought.

It is GPL-3.0, so you can read every line of it. Playback is Media3, lyrics come from LrcLib among others, and it is on F-Droid, whose build servers compile it from source and check the result matches the file published here.

These five open-source apps all play music from YouTube Music without adverts, and they share a lot of history. This page sets out the plain facts that tell them apart: where each one runs, whether it is still maintained, and where you can get it.
The five apps at a glance
Checked on 4 November 2026. Release numbers move quickly, so look at each project's own page for the newest one.

Blazify did not start from nothing. Its streaming core builds on InnerTune and on Metrolist, which grew out of it, and Blazify would not exist without the people who wrote and maintain those projects. Thank you to all of them. Because every one of these apps is GPL-3.0, that kind of building on each other's work is exactly what the licence allows, as long as the result stays open too.
What Blazify adds on top is its own design and features, and apps for iPhone, Windows and Linux. It is made by one developer, Rajendra Pandey, in Kathmandu, Nepal.
Pick it if you want the same player on Android, iPhone, Windows and Linux, or if you install apps from F-Droid, where it is built from source.
Pick it if a large community matters to you. It is active and has about 14,000 stars on GitHub.
Pick it if you want another actively maintained app, available from both F-Droid and IzzyOnDroid.
The project Metrolist grew from, and part of Blazify's base. It still installs, but there has been no release since September 2024.
Archived and read-only since July 2024. If you still use it, any of the active apps above is a safer choice.
All five are free and open source under the GPL-3.0 licence. Blazify has no paid plan, no advert, no analytics and no tracking libraries.
